title: Five of Cups: acknowledge the loss and see what remains

quickTake.upright: First acknowledge the actual loss. You do not need to hurry to turn sadness into something good.
quickTake.reversed: You may be reconnecting with life, or discovering that you still need time to work through regret.

bodyMarkdown:
Upright at a glance: First acknowledge the actual loss. You do not need to hurry to turn sadness into something good.

Reversed at a glance: You may be reconnecting with life, or discovering that you still need time to work through regret.

Comfort offered too quickly can feel like pressure to stop being sad. The Five of Cups places the spilled cups before us while leaving two others in the picture.

## Three have fallen; two are still standing

Beneath a gray sky, a figure wrapped in a long black cloak stands with head lowered, body facing the left side of the image. Three golden cups lie overturned in front of the feet, with red and green liquid on the ground. Two more cups stand upright behind the figure to the right. The figure has not turned to look at them.

A blue river crosses the background, with an arched bridge to the right and a small turreted building on the green land beyond. The cloak encloses the figure, while the river, bridge and distant dwelling draw our eyes farther away. The bridge provides a visible route, but it does not promise that crossing it will compensate for every loss. [View the card used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cups05.jpg)

The three fallen cups and the two standing ones occupy the same image; their significance need not cancel out. The river separates the figure from the distant building, and the bridge offers a route around it, not one immediately underfoot. A modern reading can therefore emphasize stages: recognize the loss first, then decide whether to move toward the resources that remain. Asking someone to “look on the bright side” immediately skips over the lowered head that is so prominent in this card.

## The source already leaves room for what remains beyond loss

The 1911 English transcription of Waite’s *The Pictorial Key to the Tarot* explicitly describes something lost and something remaining. It also lists older meanings involving an inheritance or transmission that falls short of expectations. The reversed entry includes news, connections, kinship and return, alongside illusory plans; these directions are not entirely consistent. [Waite’s entry for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktcu05.htm)

Using the reversed card to explore accepting support again and working through regret is this site’s modern reflective extension. We do not infer from a single card that an inheritance, marriage or any particular event has occurred. The person’s actual experience should be the starting point for discussion.

## Upright: make the disappointment specific

Sadness may be about more than an unsuccessful result. Effort may have gone unrecognized, or a future you had expected may no longer be possible. Trying to name what has actually been lost makes it easier to find the help you need than telling yourself to get over it.

Acknowledging loss does not mean you must remain where you are. You can feel regret while doing what today requires, and you can choose not to seek a positive meaning for now. The two standing cups can remind you to check your resources; they do not demand immediate gratitude.

## Reversed: reconnection need not happen all at once

The reversed card can help you notice a small change: being willing to reply to a friend, returning to routines you had set aside, or being able to discuss the event rather than only blaming yourself repeatedly. Such changes are small, but still worth noticing.

Another possibility is saying it is over while continuing to organize every action around undoing the old outcome. First distinguish what can still be repaired from what cannot be changed. Then decide where to make amends and where to stop spending further energy.

## Put the card back into the question and position

In a loss position, the Five of Cups can help specify what is gone: a place you hoped to secure, time shared with someone, or an expectation of yourself. In a resources position, it may prompt you to check for support still available behind you. Reversed, it can sometimes suggest renewed contact and sometimes simply reveal regret that has not yet been addressed. The distinction comes from the person’s actions and wishes. Neither orientation sets a deadline for grief, and the historical meaning of “return” does not guarantee that a particular person will come back.

## Returning to your work after an unsuccessful submission

**Original fictional example.** Xiao Cen spent three months preparing for a photography exhibition, then received notice that her work had not been selected. She lost this chance to exhibit and is troubled that friends had looked forward to attending. Her image files are intact, however, and her tutor is willing to review the work with her. Another open call has yet to begin.

Her question is, “After this rejection by the selection panel, what do I need to acknowledge first?” The Five of Cups appears upright in the position for what needs to be faced.

The three fallen cups can help her acknowledge that the exhibition opportunity really has been lost. “You learned a lot” cannot erase that fact. The two cups still standing behind the figure can correspond to the completed work and available feedback, rather than hinting at two mysterious compensations. The distant bridge suggests a transition from disappointment to a next step; she need not submit again that same day.

If her real sadness is a feeling that she has let down the family who supported her, discussing the photographs alone would miss the issue. It would be necessary to hear what meaning she had attached to this selection. If the work depends on permissions that do not allow reuse, intact files may not be usable resources either; those conditions need checking first.

She gives herself two days without major decisions, then asks her tutor for one comment on composition and one on her choice of images. She separates the feedback she receives from the criticism she imagines. Only afterward does she decide whether to revise the work for another exhibition, instead of immediately chasing another place to make the sadness go away.

## Reconnecting with an old friend without skipping the earlier hurt

**Original fictional example.** A-Ting has not seen a friend for six months after an unequal division of tasks on a trip caused a dispute. The friend recently sent a poster for a film they had watched together, without mentioning the disagreement. A-Ting misses the friend somewhat but worries that replying would imply that everything is now in the past.

The question is, “I would like to reconnect. How can I begin without repeating the old problem?” The Five of Cups appears reversed in the advice-for-repair position.

The traditional reversed themes of news and contact can frame the contact that has actually occurred. The standing cups and bridge also offer a metaphor: repair might begin with a shared experience that is still available, but the distance between them must still be crossed. The poster is a signal of contact; it does not prove that an apology has been offered or the issue resolved.

If the message is merely an event notice sent to a group, the evidence for mutual repair is weaker. If the friend later listens to the concern about shared tasks and acknowledges specific actions, there are grounds to continue. If the friend repeatedly denies the issue or pressures A-Ting to move on, distance should be maintained. Whether to reply can also be decided entirely according to A-Ting’s own wishes.

If a reply feels right, they can begin with the film, then ask for a brief conversation about the one thing that was most troubling on the trip and the arrangements needed in future. The first goal is only to understand each other, without rushing to plan another trip. Renewing contact and restoring the former degree of closeness are two decisions that can be made separately.

## Bring the understanding into today

On a sheet of paper, make three lists: “What has actually been lost,” “What I can still use,” and “What I am not ready to do yet.” They need not be equally long. Choose only one next action you are willing to take, such as preserving your files, accepting company or temporarily stopping comparisons. The bridge can wait there for you; grief does not have to end immediately to fit a card meaning.
